title: 60 SQL Practice Queries with Answers on PostgreSQL
summary: Sixty drills over an employees/departments/orders schema on PostgreSQL, ordered from basics to interview classics. Each task has a prompt, runnable solution code and the result on the sample data.

chapters.title: 60 SQL Practice Queries: PostgreSQL Drills
points: Cover: 60 queries with answers on PostgreSQL 16
Basics and filtering: 9 tasks
Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING: 8 tasks
Joins: 8 tasks
Subqueries: 8 tasks
Window functions: 9 tasks
CTEs, recursive and data-modifying: 8 tasks
Real interview scenarios: 10 tasks (nth highest salary, duplicates, running totals)
Every answer runs as written on the same sample data

chapters.title: The Sample Schema and Data
points: Describe employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hire_date) and what each column holds
Describe departments(id, name, location) and how employees.dept_id references it
Describe orders(id, employee_id, customer, amount, order_date, status) and the status values
Show the CREATE TABLE statements with primary and foreign keys
Show the INSERT rows for departments
Show the INSERT rows for employees, including a NULL manager_id and a NULL dept_id
Show the INSERT rows for orders, including an employee with no orders
Explain why the NULLs and ties are in the data: they drive the joins, window and interview drills

chapters.title: Basics and Filtering
points: Select the name and salary of every employee
List the distinct department ids used in employees
Show each employee with an annual_salary column computed as salary * 12
Return the five most recently hired employees with ORDER BY hire_date DESC LIMIT 5
Find employees in department 10 who earn more than 60000
Find employees whose salary is between 50000 and 80000 inclusive
Find employees in departments 10, 20 or 30 using IN
Find employees whose name starts with 'A' using ILIKE
Find employees with no manager using IS NULL

chapters.title: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
points: Count all rows in employees
Count employees that have a manager and show how COUNT(manager_id) differs from COUNT(*)
Show the average, minimum and maximum salary in one query
Compute total salary per department
Count employees per department sorted from largest to smallest
List departments with more than 5 employees using HAVING
Compute average order amount per employee for completed orders only, filtering with WHERE before grouping
Total order amount per month using date_trunc('month', order_date)

chapters.title: Joins
points: List each employee with their department name using INNER JOIN
List every department including those with no employees using LEFT JOIN
Find departments with no employees using LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
Show each employee next to their manager's name with a self join
Find employees who earn more than their manager
Total order amount per employee including employees with no orders, using COALESCE
Join orders, employees and departments to show order amount by department name
Pair every department with every distinct order status using CROSS JOIN

chapters.title: Subqueries
points: Find employees earning more than the company average with a scalar subquery
Find employees working in departments located in 'Austin' using IN (subquery)
Find employees who placed at least one order using EXISTS
Find employees who never placed an order using NOT EXISTS
Find the highest-paid employee in each department with a correlated subquery
Find departments whose average salary is above the company average using HAVING with a subquery
Show each employee with their order count using a scalar subquery in SELECT
Average the per-department average salaries using a derived table in FROM

chapters.title: Window Functions
points: Number employees by salary within each department using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
Rank employees by salary with RANK() and show the gaps left by ties
Return the top 3 salaries per department with DENSE_RANK()
Show each employee's salary next to their department average using AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
Show the salary change from the previously hired employee using LAG
Show each order's next order date per employee using LEAD
Compute a running total of order amount per employee ordered by order_date
Compute a 3-order moving average with ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Split employees into four salary quartiles with NTILE(4)

chapters.title: CTEs: Basic, Recursive and Data-Modifying
points: Rewrite the above-average-salary query using a WITH clause
Chain two CTEs: monthly order totals, then months above the average month
Total salary per department in a CTE, then join to departments for the name
Walk an employee hierarchy down from a given manager with WITH RECURSIVE
Compute each employee's depth in the reporting chain with a recursive level counter
Generate the numbers 1 to 10 with a recursive CTE
Archive deleted cancelled orders by chaining DELETE ... RETURNING inside a CTE into an INSERT
Force a CTE to be computed once with AS MATERIALIZED

chapters.title: Real Interview Scenarios
points: Find the second highest distinct salary
Find the 3rd highest salary with DENSE_RANK() in a subquery
Return the 3rd highest salary as NULL when it does not exist using OFFSET inside a wrapping subquery
Find duplicate employee names with their counts using GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
Delete duplicate rows keeping the lowest id using a self-join DELETE ... USING
Find managers with at least three direct reports
Pivot order amount by status into columns using SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)
Compute month-over-month revenue growth with LAG
Compute a monthly running total of revenue with a cumulative percentage
Find the median salary using PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Using = NULL instead of IS NULL, so the filter returns nothing
Filtering an aggregate in WHERE instead of HAVING
Selecting a column that is not in GROUP BY or an aggregate
Putting a right-table filter in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN, which turns it into an inner join
NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL, which matches no rows; use NOT EXISTS
Using ROW_NUMBER when ties should share a rank, or RANK when gapless ranks are needed
Running total without ORDER BY in the window, which sums the whole partition
LIMIT without ORDER BY gives nondeterministic rows

chapters.title: SQL Drills Cheatsheet
points: Clause order written: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Logical execution order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
JOIN types and which rows each keeps
EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN: when to use each
ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on tied salaries
LAG, LEAD, NTILE and frame syntax at a glance
CTE vs subquery vs recursive CTE: choosing between them
nth highest salary: DENSE_RANK vs OFFSET pattern
Duplicates: detect with GROUP BY HAVING, remove with USING
COALESCE, FILTER and date_trunc one-liners
